title: Organ Transplants
objective: After this level you can explain how organ transplants work and why matching matters.
summary: The immune system can reject a donated organ. The 1954 twin kidney transplant worked because twins match; blood and tissue matching plus immunosuppressants help everyone else.

cards.headline: Before a famous operation, two brothers were fingerprinted at a police station.
cards.body: Doctors needed proof that Richard and Ronald Herrick were truly identical twins, so they ran 17 tests. Why did being identical matter so much?

cards.headline: The body's ID check
cards.body: Your cells carry antigens, proteins on their surfaces. A donated organ carries someone else's, and the immune system can attack it. That's rejection. No two people have identical tissue antigens, except identical twins, whose tissues are genetically identical. That's why transplants between identical twins are almost never rejected. That's why the Herricks' 17 tests mattered so much.

mascot.line: Level 25's name tags again: your immune system checks the markers on cells.

cards.fact: On 23 December 1954, Richard Herrick received a kidney from his identical twin, Ronald.
cards.context: Joseph Murray's team in Boston performed the first successful human organ transplant. Murray had learned from grafting skin that tissue from an identical twin isn't rejected. Richard lived eight more years, and Murray later shared the 1990 Nobel Prize for his transplant work.

cards.headline: Matching everyone else
cards.body: Most people don't have a twin to ask. So before a transplant, doctors check blood type and tissue type in donor and recipient; the closer the match, the lower the risk of rejection. Most recipients then take immunosuppressant medicines for life to hold off the attack. Those drugs let Murray's team transplant a kidney from an unrelated donor in 1962. Today one organ donor can save up to 8 lives, and a living person can give a kidney, since people can live with one.

questions.prompt: Nearly every cell in one body carries the same DNA. Why could Ronald Herrick's kidney join Richard's body without rejection?

options.label: Brothers always match perfectly
options.rationale: Only identical twins match like that.

options.label: Identical twins are genetically identical, so their antigens match
The kidney's own DNA was removed and replaced with Richard's before surgery
options.rationale: Nothing was removed; the tissues already matched.

questions.explanation: Identical twins' tissues are genetically identical, so they carry the same tissue antigens and the immune system sees no stranger.
